source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's NVA4 campus in Sterling, Virginia publishes 11 MW of IT capacity and 128,715 square feet of technical space, a modest figure in the largest data center market in the world.

The published numbers describe a mixed colocation facility, not a purpose-built AI training hall. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 11 MW of IT load is roughly 275 racks. At 10 kW per rack, typical of older enterprise colocation, the same load is about 1,100 racks. The square footage implies a power density near 85 watts per square foot if the full technical area is loaded to the published capacity. That is plausible for a colocation hall and is not evidence of a design built for dense accelerator workloads. The operator publishes no rack count, no accelerator count, no cooling architecture, and no tenant information.

The more useful fact is how little of Virginia is measured at all. The state has 376 mapped facilities and only 29 with a published megawatt figure. NVA4 ranks 26th by published capacity among those 29, against a published state total of 2,563.4 MW. An 11 MW campus is a small increment against that total, and the true total is almost certainly larger because most facilities publish nothing. The binding constraint on AI scaling is the grid, and the grid argument depends on capacity figures that mostly do not exist in public form.

What this does not tell the reader is anything about NVA4's actual tenants, its utilization, or whether it hosts AI workloads at all. The operator lists no certifications, so nothing is published about what standards the campus has been qualified against. The address and postal code fields are empty, so the exact siting is not published either. The capacity figure is real and sourced, and it is one of a small minority of Virginia facilities for which any figure is published.
